summary: Adds an optional feature to the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP) that lets the controlling host start and stop individual test sessions by Session Identifier. The base protocol starts and stops all accepted sessions together. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Instead of one button that starts every race, you get a button per runner.

subtitle: An optional TWAMP feature that lets a controller start and stop individual test sessions by their Session Identifier.

tldr.problem: In base TWAMP, all test sessions that were requested and accepted start and stop at the same time, so a short test cannot run inside a longer one.
tldr.mechanism: A new Modes bit (value 16) and four new control commands, Start-N-Sessions, Start-N-Ack, Stop-N-Sessions and Stop-N-Ack, let the Control-Client name sessions by Session Identifier (SID).
tldr.outcome: Measurement systems can launch or end a specific test mid-run, for example a diagnostic test triggered by intermediate results. The feature is OPTIONAL and updates RFC 5357.

today: RFC 5938 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5357. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Individual Session Control
sections.content:
TWAMP, the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol defined in RFC 5357, starts all previously requested and accepted test sessions at once. Individual Session Control is an OPTIONAL feature that lets the Control-Client control sessions one by one using their Session Identifier (SID).

The RFC gives two motivations: a short TWAMP test can start or stop during a longer test, and a specific diagnostic test can begin if intermediate results show it is warranted. This memo updates RFC 5357, but a measurement system does not need it to claim compliance with that RFC.
sections.eli5: Normally every test starts and ends together, like a class lining up for one whistle. This feature lets the teacher send single students off whenever needed.

sections.title: Negotiating the Mode
sections.content:
The feature is announced through the TWAMP Modes field, a recognized extension mechanism. It takes one new bit position, bit 4, which has the value 16. A Server that supports it sets that bit in its Server Greeting; a Control-Client that wants it sets the bit in its Setup Response.

Once both sides agree, they MUST use the new start and stop commands and their acknowledgements, and MUST NOT use the original Start-Sessions and Stop-Sessions commands (2 and 3) or the acknowledgement from RFC 5357. The Control-Client must also set one bit for the chosen security mode (bits 0, 1, 2 or 3) and MAY set other feature bits, such as the reflect octets feature.
sections.eli5: Both sides first agree out loud that they will use the new buttons, and after that the old all-at-once buttons are off limits.

sections.title: The Four New Commands
sections.content:
Each new message begins with a command number and ends with a single-block HMAC. In between is a Number of Sessions field, which MUST be one or greater, followed by exactly that many 16-octet SIDs.

  • Start-N-Sessions (command 7): sent by the Control-Client to start one or more sessions. The "N" just means one or more.
  • Start-N-Ack (command 8): the Server's reply, carrying an Accept field.
  • Stop-N-Sessions (command 9): only the Control-Client can send it, and it MUST name at least one SID.
  • Stop-N-Ack (command 10): the Server's reply, a new response added to make stopping symmetric with starting.

The Server MUST answer with one or more acknowledgements, which SHOULD be sent as quickly as possible. Multiple Start-N-Sessions commands MAY be sent without waiting for acknowledgement, and they MAY arrive in any order.
sections.eli5: There are four notes: please start these runners, okay they started, please stop these runners, okay they stopped. Each note lists the runners by name.

sections.title: Partial Acceptance with Accept Codes
sections.content:
A Server might be unable to start or stop every session named in a command. So it may reply with several acknowledgements, each carrying an Accept value (defined in RFC 4656) and the SIDs it applies to. All SIDs with the same Accept code can share one acknowledgement.

The RFC's example: the Server gets a Start-N-Sessions for SIDs 1, 2, 3 and 4, and the resources for SID 3 are temporarily unavailable. It sends one Start-N-Ack with Accept = 0 for SIDs 1, 2 and 4, and another with Accept = 5 for SID 3.
sections.eli5: If you ask for four runners and one has a shoelace problem, the coach says yes for three and not yet for the fourth.

sections.title: Timers and Test Behavior
sections.content:
The Server normally suspends its optional SERVWAIT timer while test sessions are in progress. With this feature, that suspension covers the whole time that ANY session is in progress. SERVWAIT monitoring resumes after a Stop-N-Sessions has covered all the corresponding SIDs, or when REFWAIT expires on all sessions started by the control connection. An implementation that supports SERVWAIT SHOULD also implement REFWAIT.

The sender MUST manage test sessions by SID. The Session-Reflector MUST also manage accepted sessions by SID. After a Stop-N-Sessions for a SID, it MUST ignore test packets for that session and MUST NOT generate reply test packets for them. If REFWAIT is implemented, it SHOULD be enforced while any test session is in progress.
sections.eli5: The timekeeper stops checking the clock while any runner is still on the track, and starts again only when the last one is done.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned one Modes bit and four command numbers. In the "TWAMP-Control Command Numbers" registry, values 7, 8, 9 and 10 now mean Start-N-Sessions, Start-N-Ack, Stop-N-Sessions and Stop-N-Ack. In the "TWAMP-Modes" registry, value 16 (bit position 4) means Individual Session Control.

The RFC notes that the Command Numbers registry holds only 256 values and the Modes field has 32 bit positions, so both registries are to be updated only by "IETF Consensus" as in RFC 5226.
sections.eli5: The official list of button numbers got four new entries, so everyone uses the same numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds very little here. The security considerations that apply to any active measurement of live networks are relevant, and readers are pointed to the security sections of RFC 4656 and RFC 5357. The new messages are protected with the same single-block HMAC used elsewhere in the control protocol.
sections.eli5: The new notes are sealed with the same tamper-proof stamp as the old ones, and the safety rules of the older protocols still apply.
